Title: Ulcerative colitis
Focus: Authoritative Lancet seminar on UC: epidemiology, pathogenesis (genetics, barrier, microbiome, immunity), diagnosis and the full treatment ladder from 5-ASA to JAK inhibitors and S1P modulators. Key message: despite more drugs, 10-20% of patients still need colectomy, so combination therapy and precision medicine are seen as the way past the 'therapeutic ceiling'.

Title: Crohn's disease
Focus: Lancet seminar on CD describing the shift to early effective advanced therapy, treat-to-target monitoring and deeper targets (histological/transmural healing). It explicitly names future combinations of advanced therapies with diet as a direction.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Names diet-plus-drug combination as a future strategy for CD, which is the space where the Mediterranean diet could fit.

Title: The four epidemiological stages in the global evolution of inflammatory bowel disease
Focus: Influential framework describing four epidemiological stages of IBD (Emergence, Acceleration in Incidence, Compounding Prevalence, Prevalence Equilibrium). Explains why IBD is now rising quickly in newly industrialised countries in Asia, Latin America and the Middle East.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Links the global rise of IBD to westernisation, including dietary change away from traditional patterns.

Title: Temporal Trends and Socio-Demographic Disparities in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Insights from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021
Focus: Global Burden of Disease 2021 analysis (204 countries, 1990-2021, projections to 2040). Highest burden in high-SDI regions (Australasia, North America, Western Europe); incidence rising and inequalities widening, while mortality/DALYs fall.

Title: A disease-associated gene desert directs macrophage inflammation through ETS2
Focus: Major 2024 Nature discovery: a disease-associated 'gene desert' on chr21q22 controls macrophage inflammation via the transcription factor ETS2. ETS2 switches on many current drug targets at once (e.g. TNF, IL-23), and the authors identify existing drug classes (MEK inhibitors, per the full paper) that dampen this pathway, which makes it a new therapeutic target.

Title: The Role of ETS2 in Macrophage Inflammation
Focus: Follow-up review by the ETS2 discoverers explaining why ETS2 is a 'master regulator' (it drives TNF, IL-23, IL-1β and TL1A signalling) and what hurdles exist to drugging it. It shows how genetics is now pointing to targets above the level of single cytokines.

Title: Environmental risk factors of inflammatory bowel disease: toward a strategy of preventative health
Focus: Review of 79 meta-analyses on modifiable environmental risk factors. Risk: smoking, Western diet, ultra-processed foods, early-life antibiotics. Protective: breastfeeding, Mediterranean-type diets rich in fibre, plant foods and fish, physical activity. It frames IBD as partly preventable.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Lists the Mediterranean diet among the protective, modifiable factors and calls for prevention trials.

Title: Serum Biomarkers Identify Patients Who Will Develop Inflammatory Bowel Diseases Up to 5 Years Before Diagnosis
Focus: PREDICTS study using archived serum from 200 people later diagnosed with CD and 199 with UC. A panel of antibodies and proteins predicted CD up to 5 years before diagnosis with high accuracy, but did not predict UC. This is the basis of the 'pre-clinical IBD' concept and of prevention trials, including dietary ones.

Title: STRIDE-II: An Update on the Selecting Therapeutic Targets in Inflammatory Bowel Disease (STRIDE) Initiative of the International Organization for the Study of IBD (IOIBD): Determining Therapeutic Goals for Treat-to-Target strategies in IBD
Focus: STRIDE-II (IOIBD) sets the treat-to-target goals used worldwide. Short-term: symptom response and normalised CRP/calprotectin. Long-term: clinical remission, endoscopic healing, restored quality of life and absence of disability; in children, normal growth. Transmural healing (CD) and histological healing (UC) are not formal targets but measure the depth of remission.

Title: A biomarker-stratified comparison of top-down versus accelerated step-up treatment strategies for patients with newly diagnosed Crohn's disease (PROFILE): a multicentre, open-label randomised controlled trial
Focus: PROFILE RCT (386 newly diagnosed CD patients). Top-down infliximab plus immunomodulator from diagnosis gave 79% sustained steroid- and surgery-free remission at week 48, against 15% with accelerated step-up. The biomarker (PredictSURE) did not identify who benefits. Landmark evidence for treating early.

Title: Long-term outcomes of top-down therapy versus a conventional step-up strategy in adults newly diagnosed with Crohn's disease: 5-year follow-up of the PROFILE trial
Article type: Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial; Comparative Study
Focus: PROFILE 5-year follow-up. Disease progression occurred in 17% of patients started on step-up against 7% on top-down (aHR 2.46), with no difference in serious infections or cancers. Authors suggest a disease-modifying effect of early anti-TNF.

Title: Anti-tumor necrosis factor treatment from diagnosis is more effective and less costly than conventional "step-up" care for patients with active Crohn's disease: a cost-effectiveness analysis from the PROFILE trial
Focus: Health-economic analysis of PROFILE: top-down anti-TNF from diagnosis was both more effective and cheaper over 5 years (dominant in 98.7% of simulations).

Title: AGA Living Clinical Practice Guideline on Pharmacological Management of Moderate-to-Severe Ulcerative Colitis
Focus: AGA 2024 living guideline for moderate-to-severe UC (14 recommendations). Recommends many advanced therapies (infliximab, golimumab, vedolizumab, tofacitinib, upadacitinib, ustekinumab, ozanimod, etrasimod, risankizumab, guselkumab; and suggests adalimumab, filgotinib, mirikizumab). Positions them by prior advanced-therapy exposure and suggests early advanced and/or immunomodulator therapy over gradual step-up after 5-ASA failure.

Title: Comparative Efficacy of Advanced Therapies for Management of Moderate-to-Severe Ulcerative Colitis: 2024 American Gastroenterological Association Evidence Synthesis
Article type: Systematic Review; Comparative Study; Network Meta-Analysis
Focus: Network meta-analysis underpinning the AGA UC guideline: ranks drugs for biologic-naive and biologic-exposed patients. Upadacitinib, tofacitinib and ustekinumab ranked highest after prior biologic exposure.

Title: AGA Living Clinical Practice Guideline on the Pharmacologic Management of Moderate-to-Severe Crohn's Disease
Focus: AGA 2025 living guideline for moderate-to-severe CD (16 recommendations). For advanced-therapy-naive patients it suggests 'higher-efficacy' agents (infliximab, adalimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab). It prefers infliximab plus thiopurine combination, and recommends starting advanced therapy early instead of step therapy.

Title: Comparative Efficacy of Advanced Therapies for Management of Moderate-to-Severe Crohn's Disease: 2025 AGA Evidence Synthesis
Article type: Systematic Review; Comparative Study; Network Meta-Analysis
Focus: Updated network meta-analysis for the AGA CD guideline. Moderate-certainty evidence favours risankizumab and guselkumab over vedolizumab and ustekinumab among active comparators.

Title: ECCO Guidelines on Therapeutics in Crohn's Disease: Medical Treatment
Focus: ECCO 2024 guideline on medical therapy of CD, the European reference for induction and maintenance with conventional and advanced therapies. (PubMed lists no abstract; open the DOI for the full recommendations.)

Title: ECCO Guidelines on Therapeutics in Ulcerative Colitis: Medical Treatment
Focus: Newest ECCO guideline on medical treatment of UC (2026), the current European reference for UC drug therapy. (PubMed lists no abstract; open the DOI for the full recommendations.)

Title: ECCO-ESGAR-ESP-IBUS Guideline on Diagnostics and Monitoring of Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Part 1
Focus: Joint ECCO-ESGAR-ESP-IBUS 2025 guideline on how to diagnose and monitor IBD: endoscopy, intestinal ultrasound, MRI, histology, biomarkers, and special situations (pregnancy, post-operative, cancer surveillance).

Title: Management of pediatric Crohn's disease: an ECCO-ESPGHAN guideline update
Focus: 2026 ECCO-ESPGHAN paediatric CD guideline. Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) or the CD Exclusion Diet with partial enteral nutrition are preferred induction options. Targets are endoscopic remission, normal growth and less bowel damage.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Paediatric guidelines now put dietary therapy (EEN/CDED) first-line for inducing remission in CD.

Title: EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF ADVANCED THERAPIES AS INDUCTION THERAPY FOR ULCERATIVE COLITIS: AN UPDATED SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND NETWORK META-ANALYSIS
Focus: 2026 network meta-analysis of advanced therapies for UC induction. Upadacitinib is most effective overall; obefazimod and SC guselkumab rank highly in therapy-naive patients; anti-p19 drugs (risankizumab, guselkumab, mirikizumab) have the most favourable safety profile.

Title: Risankizumab as induction therapy for Crohn's disease: results from the phase 3 ADVANCE and MOTIVATE induction trials
Focus: ADVANCE and MOTIVATE, phase 3 IV induction in CD. Risankizumab 600 mg gave CDAI remission of 45% against 25% for placebo, and endoscopic response of 40% against 12% at week 12 (ADVANCE). Both doses met all co-primary endpoints in both trials.

Title: Risankizumab as maintenance therapy for moderately to severely active Crohn's disease: results from the multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, withdrawal phase 3 FORTIFY maintenance trial
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: FORTIFY maintenance in CD. SC risankizumab 360 mg every 8 weeks gave CDAI remission of 52% against 41% on withdrawal, and endoscopic response of 47% against 22% at week 52.

Title: Risankizumab for Ulcerative Colitis: Two Randomized Clinical Trials
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: INSPIRE and COMMAND (JAMA 2024), risankizumab for UC. Induction clinical remission was 20.3% against 6.2%. Maintenance remission at week 52 was 40.2% (180 mg) and 37.6% (360 mg) against 25.1%. No new safety risks.

Title: Mirikizumab as Induction and Maintenance Therapy for Ulcerative Colitis
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: LUCENT-1 and LUCENT-2 (NEJM 2023), mirikizumab for UC. Clinical remission was 24.2% against 13.3% at week 12, and 49.9% against 25.1% at maintenance week 40. Also improved bowel urgency.

Title: Efficacy and safety of mirikizumab in patients with moderately-to-severely active Crohn's disease: a phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled and active-controlled, treat-through study
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Randomized Controlled Trial; Multicenter Study
Focus: VIVID-1 (Lancet 2024), mirikizumab for CD (treat-through, with placebo and ustekinumab arms). Endoscopic-response composite was 38.0% against 9.0%, and CDAI-remission composite 45.4% against 19.6%.

Title: Guselkumab in patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (QUASAR): phase 3 double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled induction and maintenance studies
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study
Focus: QUASAR (Lancet 2024), guselkumab for UC. Induction remission was 23% against 8%. Week-44 remission was 50% (200 mg q4w) and 45% (100 mg q8w) against 19%.

Title: Efficacy and safety of intravenous induction and subcutaneous maintenance therapy with guselkumab for patients with Crohn's disease (GALAXI-2 and GALAXI-3): 48-week results from two phase 3, randomised, placebo and active comparator-controlled, double-blind, triple-dummy trials
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study
Focus: GALAXI-2 and GALAXI-3 (Lancet 2025), guselkumab for CD with IV induction and SC maintenance, compared with placebo and ustekinumab. Clinical response at week 12 plus remission at week 48 reached 47-55% against 12-13% on placebo. Superior to ustekinumab on multiple week-48 endpoints.

Title: Efficacy and Safety of Guselkumab Subcutaneous Induction and Maintenance in Participants With Moderately to Severely Active Crohn's Disease: Results From the Phase 3 GRAVITI Study
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study
Focus: GRAVITI (Gastroenterology 2025): guselkumab given subcutaneously for both induction and maintenance in CD (no IV infusion needed). Clinical remission and endoscopic response were clearly superior to placebo in biologic-naive and biologic-experienced patients.

Title: Risankizumab versus Ustekinumab for Moderate-to-Severe Crohn's Disease
Article type: Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Comparative Study; Equivalence Trial
Focus: SEQUENCE (NEJM 2024) in anti-TNF-failed CD. Risankizumab was non-inferior to ustekinumab for week-24 clinical remission (58.6% vs 39.5%) and superior for week-48 endoscopic remission (31.8% vs 16.2%). This is the first head-to-head win for an IL-23 p19 drug.

Title: Ustekinumab versus adalimumab for induction and maintenance therapy in biologic-naive patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 3b trial
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: SEAVUE (Lancet 2022) in biologic-naive CD. Ustekinumab and adalimumab monotherapy were similarly effective (week-52 remission 65% vs 61%). Either is a reasonable first biologic.

Title: Vedolizumab versus Adalimumab for Moderate-to-Severe Ulcerative Colitis
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Comparative Study; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: VARSITY (NEJM 2019), the first head-to-head biologic trial in IBD. In UC, vedolizumab beat adalimumab for clinical remission (31.3% vs 22.5%) and endoscopic improvement, but not for steroid-free remission.

Title: Upadacitinib as induction and maintenance therapy for moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis: results from three phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, randomised trials
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: U-ACHIEVE and U-ACCOMPLISH (Lancet 2022), upadacitinib (JAK1) for UC. Induction remission was 26-34% against 4-5%. Maintenance remission was 42% (15 mg) and 52% (30 mg) against 12%. It is one of the most effective UC drugs in network meta-analyses.

Title: Upadacitinib Induction and Maintenance Therapy for Crohn's Disease
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: U-EXCEL, U-EXCEED and U-ENDURE (NEJM 2023), upadacitinib for CD. Remission was 49.5% against 29.1% and endoscopic response 45.5% against 13.1% (U-EXCEL). Herpes zoster, liver enzyme changes and a few GI perforations were noted.

Title: Filgotinib as induction and maintenance therapy for ulcerative colitis (SELECTION): a phase 2b/3 double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase II; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: SELECTION (Lancet 2021): filgotinib 200 mg (JAK1-preferential) induced and maintained remission in UC and was well tolerated.

Title: Ozanimod as Induction and Maintenance Therapy for Ulcerative Colitis
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: True North (NEJM 2021): ozanimod (S1P receptor modulator) for UC. Remission was 18.4% against 6.0% at induction and 37.0% against 18.5% in maintenance. It works by trapping lymphocytes in lymph nodes.

Title: Etrasimod as induction and maintenance therapy for ulcerative colitis (ELEVATE): two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 studies
Focus: ELEVATE UC 52 and UC 12 (Lancet 2023): once-daily etrasimod (S1P1,4,5) for UC. Remission was 27% against 7% at week 12 and 32% against 7% at week 52. No deaths or malignancies.

Title: Subcutaneous Infliximab (CT-P13 SC) as Maintenance Therapy for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Two Randomized Phase 3 Trials (LIBERTY)
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase III; Randomized Controlled Trial; Multicenter Study
Focus: LIBERTY (Gastroenterology 2024): subcutaneous infliximab (CT-P13 SC) maintenance after IV induction. Week-54 CD remission was 62.3% against 32.1%, and UC remission 43.2% against 20.8%. This allows home self-injection of infliximab.

Title: Guselkumab plus golimumab combination therapy versus guselkumab or golimumab monotherapy in patients with ulcerative colitis (VEGA): a randomised, double-blind, controlled, phase 2, proof-of-concept trial
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase II
Focus: VEGA (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2023), a proof-of-concept trial combining two biologics (guselkumab plus golimumab) in UC. Week-12 clinical response was 83% on the combination against 61% on golimumab and 75% on guselkumab alone. This launched the 'advanced combination therapy' era.

Title: Phase 2 Trial of Anti-TL1A Monoclonal Antibody Tulisokibart for Ulcerative Colitis
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase II; Multicenter Study
Focus: ARTEMIS-UC (NEJM 2024): tulisokibart for UC. Clinical remission was 26% against 1% at week 12 (cohort 1). A genetic-based companion test aimed to identify patients more likely to respond (32% vs 11% in test-positive patients).

Title: Safety and efficacy of the anti-TL1A monoclonal antibody tulisokibart for Crohn's disease: a phase 2a induction trial
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase II; Multicenter Study
Focus: APOLLO-CD (phase 2a, open-label): tulisokibart in largely biologic-experienced CD. Endoscopic response was 26% at week 12. A placebo-controlled phase 3 trial is underway.

Title: Anti-TL1A antibody, afimkibart, in moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis (TUSCANY-2): a multicentre, double-blind, treat-through, multi-dose, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial
Article type: Multicenter Study; Clinical Trial, Phase II; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: TUSCANY-2 (phase 2b): afimkibart (RVT-3101) in UC. The primary endpoint (total Mayo remission) narrowly missed significance, but modified-Mayo remission was 30-35% against 12% on placebo, which supported further development.

Title: Efficacy and safety of duvakitug in patients with ulcerative colitis (RELIEVE UCCD): a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase II; Multicenter Study
Focus: RELIEVE UCCD (phase 2b, 2026): duvakitug in UC. Week-14 clinical remission was 36% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) against 20% on placebo, with no safety concerns.

Title: Efficacy and safety of duvakitug in patients with Crohn's disease (RELIEVE UCCD): a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase II; Multicenter Study
Focus: RELIEVE UCCD (phase 2b, 2026): duvakitug in CD. Week-14 endoscopic response was 26% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) against 13% on placebo, with no safety concerns.

Title: Review Article: TL1A Inhibitors in IBD - Mechanistic Rationale and Clinical Evidence
Focus: 2026 review of TL1A/DR3 biology and clinical data. TL1A links mucosal immunity to fibroblast activation, so inhibitors could target the 'inflammation-fibrosis continuum' that current drugs miss.

Title: ABX464 (obefazimod) for moderate-to-severe, active ulcerative colitis: a phase 2b, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled induction trial and 48 week, open-label extension
Focus: Phase 2b in UC (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022). All doses of oral ABX464 (25, 50, 100 mg) significantly reduced the modified Mayo score against placebo at week 8. Headache was the most common side effect.

Title: Obefazimod in patients with moderate-to-severely active ulcerative colitis: efficacy and safety analysis from the 96-week open-label maintenance phase 2b study
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase II; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: 96-week open-label maintenance of obefazimod 50 mg in UC. Clinical remission was 54.8% at week 48 and 52.5% at week 96, and no new safety risks emerged over 2 years.

Title: [Not peer-reviewed] ABTECT phase 3 programme of obefazimod in moderate-to-severe UC: company topline results
Focus: Phase 3 ABTECT-1 and ABTECT-2 induction trials. Obefazimod 50 mg once daily gave a pooled placebo-adjusted clinical remission of 16.4% at week 8 (p<0.0001). In the 44-week maintenance trial (n=580), clinical remission was 50.8% (25 mg) and 51.3% (50 mg) against 10.4% on placebo. The company planned an FDA filing for UC in late Q4 2026. Caveat: the company's Part 2 release refers to safety findings reported after Part 1, so read the full releases and the eventual peer-reviewed paper.

Title: Oral Peptide Therapeutics as an Emerging Treatment Modality in Immune-Mediated Inflammatory Diseases: A Narrative Review
Focus: Review of oral peptide drugs for immune-mediated diseases, centred on icotrokinra (JNJ-2113), the first oral peptide that blocks the IL-23 receptor. Icotrokinra has since been approved by the FDA for plaque psoriasis (2026, brand 'Icotyde'; see PMID 42433845) and is in phase 3 for UC (ICONIC-UC).

Title: [Not peer-reviewed] ANTHEM-UC phase 2b trial of oral icotrokinra in moderate-to-severe UC: company results
Focus: 252 patients, three once-daily oral doses. All doses met the primary endpoint of clinical response at week 12. With 400 mg, clinical response was 63.5% against 27% and clinical remission 30.2% against 11.1% on placebo. Adverse events were similar to placebo. Results kept improving to week 28, and phase 3 ICONIC-UC has started. If confirmed, this would be an IL-23-pathway drug in pill form.

Title: A Phase 2 Study of MORF-057, an Oral α4β7 Integrin Inhibitor in Moderately to Severely Active Ulcerative Colitis
Article type: Clinical Trial, Phase II; Multicenter Study
Focus: Open-label, single-arm phase 2a study of MORF-057, an oral small-molecule α4β7-integrin inhibitor, essentially an 'oral vedolizumab'. It reduced the Robarts Histopathology Index in UC (22.9% histologic remission at week 12), with effects sustained to week 52 and good tolerability.

Title: Gut-directed therapeutics in inflammatory bowel disease
Focus: Review of 'gut-directed' therapeutics: drugs that act mainly in the intestine to reduce systemic side effects. Covers gut-selective antibodies, locally acting small molecules, microbiome products and new delivery systems (engineered yeast, hydrogels, nanoparticles).

Title: Lyophilised oral faecal microbiota transplantation for ulcerative colitis (LOTUS): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
Focus: LOTUS RCT (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022): antibiotics followed by oral lyophilised (capsule) FMT induced remission in active UC. All patients who continued FMT stayed in clinical, endoscopic and histological remission at week 56.

Title: Comparative Effectiveness and Safety of Fecal Microbiota Transplantation in Ulcerative Colitis: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Focus: 2026 meta-analysis of FMT in UC. FMT improves induction clinical and endoscopic remission without more adverse events. Route matters: colonoscopy plus enema was best, while oral and nasoduodenal results were imprecise.

Title: Mechanistic insights into fecal microbiota transplantation for the treatment of ulcerative colitis: analysis of the STOP-Colitis trial
Focus: Mechanistic analysis of the STOP-Colitis RCT. Colonic FMT beat nasogastric delivery. Responders engrafted immunomodulatory bacteria and showed more mucosal regulatory T cells with fewer Th17 cells, which supports designing defined bacterial consortia.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Shows that changing the gut microbiome can calm colitis, the same mechanism proposed for the Mediterranean diet's benefits.

Title: Darvadstrocel in Patients With Crohn's Disease With Complex Perianal Fistulas: The ADMIRE CD II Phase 3 Randomized Trial
Article type: Randomized Controlled Trial; Clinical Trial, Phase III; Multicenter Study
Focus: ADMIRE CD II (Gastroenterology 2026), an important negative result. Darvadstrocel (adipose-derived stem cells) for complex perianal fistulas did not beat placebo for combined remission at week 24 (48.8% vs 46.3%). This tempers enthusiasm for local stem-cell therapy.

Title: Anti-fibrotic therapy in Crohn's disease: hype or reality-can intestinal fibrosis be targeted effectively?
Focus: Review asking whether intestinal fibrosis (strictures) can be treated with drugs. Covers ontunisertib (clinical data), anti-TL1A and obefazimod (preclinical anti-fibrotic signals), and lessons from lung and liver fibrosis drug development.

Title: Drug Development in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases: What Is Next?
Focus: Overview of 'what's next' in IBD drug development: anti-TL1A, obefazimod, NX-13, RIPK inhibitors and the IL-23 p19 class. Emphasises patient stratification and positioning of therapies.

Title: Results of the Ninth Scientific Workshop of the European Crohn's and Colitis Organisation (ECCO): artificial intelligence in endoscopy, radiology, and histology in inflammatory bowel disease diagnostics
Focus: ECCO scientific workshop on artificial intelligence in endoscopy, radiology and histology for IBD. AI can automate disease-activity scoring and may reveal new biology, but needs better datasets and reporting standards.

Title: European Crohn's and Colitis Organisation consensus on dietary management of inflammatory bowel disease
Focus: The first ECCO consensus on dietary management of IBD (J Crohns Colitis 2025;19(9):jjaf122). Five working groups covered diet to induce remission, diet to maintain remission, comorbidities, nutritional assessment and prevention. According to ECCO and secondary summaries, every person with IBD should have access to an IBD-experienced dietitian; patients should follow general healthy-eating guidance unless an IBD professional prescribes a specific diet; EEN and CDED with partial enteral nutrition are options to induce remission in CD; and the Mediterranean diet and limited red/processed meat 'can be considered' to maintain remission in UC. A 2026 commentary (PMID 41329464, DOI 10.1093/ecco-jcc/jjaf220) discusses implementing it in clinics. Check the exact wording and evidence grades in the full text.
Link to Mediterranean diet: ECCO 2025 supports the Mediterranean diet (with less red/processed meat) as an option to maintain remission in UC.

Title: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diet and Nutritional Therapies in Patients With Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Expert Review
Focus: AGA Clinical Practice Update on diet (Gastroenterology 2024), 12 best-practice statements. #1: unless contraindicated, ALL patients with IBD should be advised to follow a Mediterranean diet. A diet low in red/processed meat may reduce UC flares. Texture modification is advised for strictures. EEN and CDED are options for CD. Screen for malnutrition, vitamin D, iron and B12 deficiency. A dietitian should be part of care.
Link to Mediterranean diet: The strongest guideline endorsement of the Mediterranean diet as the default background diet for everyone with IBD.

Title: ESPEN guideline on Clinical Nutrition in inflammatory bowel disease
Focus: ESPEN 2023 guideline (71 recommendations) on clinical nutrition in IBD: malnutrition screening, micronutrients, enteral and parenteral nutrition, peri-operative nutrition, and diet in active and quiescent disease.

Title: Dietary Guidance From the International Organization for the Study of Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
Focus: IOIBD expert dietary guidance (2020) on which foods and additives to increase or reduce to control and prevent relapse. As summarised by Magro et al. (2024, PMID 38617734), it advises regular fruit and vegetables, natural omega-3 sources (UC), and reducing saturated, trans and dairy fat, processed foods rich in maltodextrin, some additives, and sweeteners such as sucralose and saccharin. Its 'eat more / eat less' lists closely mirror a Mediterranean pattern.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Its food-level advice essentially describes a Mediterranean-style, minimally processed diet.

Title: Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet Plus Partial Enteral Nutrition Induces Sustained Remission in a Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: Paediatric RCT (Gastroenterology 2019): the CD Exclusion Diet (CDED) plus partial enteral nutrition (PEN) was better tolerated than EEN and gave more sustained remission at week 12, with favourable microbiome changes.

Title: The Crohn's disease exclusion diet for induction and maintenance of remission in adults with mild-to-moderate Crohn's disease (CDED-AD): an open-label, pilot, randomised trial
Focus: CDED in adults (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022, pilot RCT). CDED with or without PEN induced and maintained remission in biologic-naive mild-to-moderate CD, with some patients reaching endoscopic remission.

Title: Meta-Analysis: Crohn's Disease Exclusion Diet for Induction and Maintenance in Crohn's Disease
Focus: 2026 meta-analysis of 17 CDED studies. Pooled clinical remission was 69% at 6-8 weeks. CDED outperformed control diets (OR 2.58), and specifically outperformed the Mediterranean diet (OR 3.95) for induction. Maintenance OR was 2.73.
Link to Mediterranean diet: For inducing remission in active CD, CDED appears more effective than the Mediterranean diet (but the evidence comes from few small studies).

Title: Exclusive enteral nutrition versus the Crohn's disease exclusion diet for remission induction in pediatric Crohn's disease: 52-week study
Focus: Paediatric comparison of EEN against CDED with 52-week follow-up. Efficacy, adherence, CRP/calprotectin normalisation and longer-term outcomes (flares, need for biologics or surgery) were similar.

Title: Treatment of Active Crohn's Disease With an Ordinary Food-based Diet That Replicates Exclusive Enteral Nutrition
Focus: CD-TREAT (Gastroenterology 2019): an ordinary-food diet designed to replicate EEN. It reproduced EEN's microbiome effects, reduced gut inflammation in rats, and 60% of treated children entered remission.

Title: Whole Food Diet Induces Remission in Children and Young Adults With Mild to Moderate Crohn's Disease and Is More Tolerable Than Exclusive Enteral Nutrition: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: TASTI-MM RCT (Gastroenterology 2025): the 'Tasty&Healthy' whole-food diet (no processed food, gluten, red meat or dairy; no formula) against EEN in children and young adults. It was much better tolerated (88% vs 52%), had similar efficacy, and improved microbiome diversity, while EEN reduced it.

Title: Association of ultra-processed food intake with risk of inflammatory bowel disease: prospective cohort study
Focus: PURE prospective cohort across 21 low-, middle- and high-income countries (BMJ 2021). Higher ultra-processed food intake was associated with higher IBD risk (HR 1.82 for ≥5 servings/day vs <1). Red meat, dairy and fruit/vegetables were not associated with risk.

Title: A Diet Low in Red and Processed Meat Does Not Reduce Rate of Crohn's Disease Flares
Focus: FACES RCT (Gastroenterology 2019): in CD in remission, cutting red and processed meat did NOT reduce time to symptomatic relapse. Important evidence against over-restrictive 'no meat' advice in CD.

Title: Impact of diet on inflammatory bowel disease risk: systematic review, meta-analyses and implications for prevention
Focus: 2025 meta-analysis of 72 prospective cohorts (more than 2 million people). Inflammatory diet (HR 1.63) and UPF (HR 1.71) raised CD risk; high fibre (HR 0.53), Mediterranean diet (HR 0.59) and minimally processed foods lowered it. No consistent dietary links were found for UC.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Pooled prospective data: high Mediterranean-diet adherence is associated with about 40% lower risk of developing CD.

Title: Dietary Interventions for the Treatment of Inflammatory Bowel Diseases: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
Focus: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 controlled solid-food diet trials (Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2023). Certainty of evidence is low or very low overall. The Mediterranean diet was similar to SCD in CD, and PEN may help induction and maintenance. Reducing red meat or refined carbohydrate did not prevent CD relapse.

Title: Using Diet to Treat Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Systematic Review
Focus: AJG 2024 systematic review of 10 diets for active adult IBD, with practical sample meal plans. Common elements are whole foods, exclusion of ultra-processed foods, and elimination followed by reintroduction. Evidence remains limited.

Title: Diet, Food, and Nutritional Exposures and Inflammatory Bowel Disease or Progression of Disease: an Umbrella Review
Focus: Umbrella review (Adv Nutr 2024): red/processed meat, processed foods and refined sugar are linked to higher IBD incidence and progression; vegetables, fruit and fibre (especially for CD) are protective. Mediterranean, vegetarian and SCD patterns are associated with lower incidence and progression.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Lists the Mediterranean diet among patterns associated with lower incidence and progression.

Title: Efficacy of Whole-Food Based Anti-inflammatory Dietary Interventions in the Management of Ulcerative Colitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Focus: 2025 meta-analysis of whole-food anti-inflammatory diets in UC. In active disease they improved clinical response (RR 1.82). In remission they lowered faecal calprotectin by about 210 µg/g but did not significantly change relapse rates.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Mediterranean-style anti-inflammatory diets work as a complement to conventional UC therapy.

Title: Anti-Inflammatory Diet Prevents Subclinical Colonic Inflammation and Alters Metabolomic Profile of Ulcerative Colitis Patients in Clinical Remission
Focus: RCT in UC in remission: an 'anti-inflammatory diet' (more fibre, probiotics, antioxidants and omega-3; less red/processed meat and added sugar) prevented subclinical inflammation (calprotectin <150 in 69% vs 37% on Canada's Food Guide). It also increased beneficial bacteria (Bifidobacteriaceae, Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae).

Title: Precision nutrition for the prevention and management of inflammatory bowel disease
Focus: Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology 2026: framework for 'precision nutrition' in IBD. It moves stepwise from phenotype-based advice, to omics-based subgroups, to fully integrated personalised diets using multi-omics, biomarkers and AI. This is where diet research in IBD is heading.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Suggests future Mediterranean-diet advice could be personalised (e.g. by microbiome or metabolomic profile).

Title: Adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with a lower risk of later-onset Crohn's disease: results from two large prospective cohort studies
Focus: Swedish cohorts, 83,147 adults followed 17 years (Gut 2020). High MD adherence was associated with a 58% lower risk of later-onset CD (HR 0.42) but had no effect on UC. About 12% of later-onset CD cases could be attributable to poor MD adherence.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Key prospective evidence that MD may help prevent CD.

Title: Diet Quality and Risk of Older-onset Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis
Focus: Same Swedish cohorts, comparing several diet-quality scores. The healthful plant-based index (HR 0.52) and modified MD (HR 0.58) were linked to lower older-onset CD risk; no score predicted UC. Different healthy patterns can work, so choice can follow food culture.
Link to Mediterranean diet: MD is one of several interchangeable healthy patterns linked to lower CD risk.

Title: Healthy eating patterns associated with reduced risk of inflammatory bowel disease by lowering low-grade inflammation: evidence from a large prospective cohort study
Focus: UK Biobank, 197,391 participants (BMC Med 2024). Higher Alternate MD and HEI-2015 scores were associated with lower CD (not UC) risk. Part of the protection (about 8-13%) was mediated through lower systemic low-grade inflammation.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Suggests MD protects partly by lowering systemic inflammation.

Title: Pre-Illness Index-Based Dietary Patterns and Inflammatory Bowel Disease Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Focus: 2025 meta-analysis of pre-illness, index-based dietary patterns. Mediterranean and other healthy patterns reduce IBD risk, and pro-inflammatory diets increase it; effects vary by region and age.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Pooled evidence that MD lowers IBD risk.

Title: Efficacy of Mediterranean Diet for the primary prevention of autoimmune diseases: A systematic review and meta-analysis featured in the Italian National Guidelines "La Dieta Mediterranea"
Focus: Counter-point: a meta-analysis for the Italian National Guidelines found NO significant association between high MD adherence and incident CD (RR 0.95) or UC (RR 1.02). Protective links were seen for multiple sclerosis and Sjögren's. Certainty was low, which shows the prevention evidence is still inconsistent.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Balancing evidence: MD's preventive effect for IBD is not certain.

Title: A Randomized Trial Comparing the Specific Carbohydrate Diet to a Mediterranean Diet in Adults With Crohn's Disease
Article type: Comparative Study; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
Focus: DINE-CD (Gastroenterology 2021), the largest diet RCT in adult CD (n=194; meals provided for 6 weeks). The Specific Carbohydrate Diet was NOT superior to MD for symptomatic remission (46.5% vs 43.5%). CRP response was rare with either diet. Because MD is easier and healthier, the authors suggest MD may be preferred for most patients with mild-to-moderate CD symptoms.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Landmark RCT: MD is as good as the more restrictive SCD for symptoms in CD.

Title: A Mediterranean Diet Pattern Improves Intestinal Inflammation Concomitant with Reshaping of the Bacteriome in Ulcerative Colitis: A Randomised Controlled Trial
Focus: RCT in quiescent UC (J Crohns Colitis 2023): 12 weeks of MD against a habitual Canadian diet. Calprotectin >100 µg/g was found in 20% of the MD group against 75% of controls. MD raised faecal short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, acetate) and protective microbes, and was well tolerated.
Link to Mediterranean diet: RCT evidence that MD helps keep UC quiet, with a microbiome mechanism.

Title: Dietary adherence to the Mediterranean diet pattern in a randomized clinical trial of patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis
Focus: Adherence analysis of the same UC trial: with dietitian education patients achieved high MD adherence without more bowel symptoms. Some nutrients were still inadequate (calcium, iron, vitamin D, vitamin E, choline, fibre in men), so tailored education is needed.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Practical tips: MD is tolerable in UC, but watch calcium, iron and vitamin D.

Title: Adherence to the Mediterranean Diet Improved Clinical Scores and Inflammatory Markers in Children with Active Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Randomized Trial
Focus: Paediatric RCT (J Inflamm Res 2022) in children with mild-to-moderate active IBD on standard therapy. Those following MD for 12 weeks had greater falls in PCDAI and PUCAI and in CRP, calprotectin, TNF-α, IL-17, IL-12 and IL-13 than controls.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Shows MD as an add-on to standard drug therapy, lowering TNF-α among other markers, in children.

Title: Multidimensional Impact of Mediterranean Diet on IBD Patients
Focus: Prospective study of 142 adults with UC or CD (Inflamm Bowel Dis 2021). After 6 months of MD: lower BMI and waist, less liver steatosis, better quality of life, and fewer patients with active disease among those on STABLE drug therapy.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Supports MD as an adjunct to unchanged medication, with metabolic benefits (fatty liver, weight).

Title: Effects of Mediterranean Diet, Curcumin, and Resveratrol on Mild-to-Moderate Active Ulcerative Colitis: A Multicenter Randomized Clinical Trial
Focus: Three-arm RCT in mild-to-moderate active UC (Nutrients 2024): MD alone, MD plus curcumin, or MD plus resveratrol for 8 weeks. All arms reduced disease activity and inflammation and improved quality of life; the supplements added little over MD alone.
Link to Mediterranean diet: MD itself drove improvement in active UC; supplements gave no clear extra benefit.

Title: The use of the Crohn's disease exclusion diet (CDED) in adults with Crohn's disease: A randomized controlled trial
Focus: Open-label RCT in adult mild-to-moderate CD (Eur J Clin Invest 2025): CDED against MD as control. Remission was 70.8% vs 38.1% at week 12 and 79.2% vs 42.9% at week 24, favouring CDED, with improved body composition.
Link to Mediterranean diet: For ACTIVE CD, CDED beat MD. MD is better positioned as a maintenance or background diet.

Title: Effect of modified Mediterranean diet supplemented with partial enteral nutrition in post-surgical patients with Crohn's disease: a pilot clinical trial
Focus: Pilot RCT after CD surgery (Br J Nutr 2026). A modified MD plus partial enteral nutrition gave quality of life and nutritional status comparable to exclusive enteral nutrition, so it may be a more palatable post-operative alternative.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Modified MD plus PEN as a real-food option after surgery.

Title: Effectiveness of a novel diet in attenuation of clinical activity of disease in patients with ulcerative colitis: a randomized, clinical trial
Focus: RCT in active mild-to-moderate UC (Sci Rep 2024): a combined Mediterranean plus low-FODMAP diet with partial enteral nutrition for 6 weeks lowered disease activity and improved quality of life compared with a regular diet.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Shows MD can be adapted (e.g. low-FODMAP) for symptomatic patients.

Title: Mechanistic Implications of the Mediterranean Diet in Patients With Newly Diagnosed Crohn's Disease: Multiomic Results From a Prospective Cohort
Focus: Prospective multi-omic cohort of 271 newly diagnosed CD patients (Gastroenterology 2025). Higher MD adherence was associated with an uncomplicated course and lower CDAI, CRP and calprotectin. Biologically it went with more SCFA-producing commensals such as Faecalibacterium and with fewer CD-associated species (E. coli, R. gnavus), primary bile acids and ceramides.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Best mechanistic human data: MD is linked to a less dysbiotic, lower-bile-acid gut environment in early CD.

Title: Distinct microbial mediators link diet to inflammation in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis
Focus: Longitudinal shotgun metagenomics with causal mediation (Gut 2026). Diet quality affects inflammation through the microbiome, differently by disease. In UC, Mediterranean-like diets lowered CRP via greater microbial richness and SCFA functions; in CD, specific taxa and metabolites mediated the benefits.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Directly shows that the anti-inflammatory effect of Mediterranean-like diets in UC runs through the microbiome.

Title: Long-term dietary patterns are associated with pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory features of the gut microbiome
Focus: Gut 2021, 1,425 people (healthy, IBS, CD, UC). Processed and animal foods were associated with pro-inflammatory microbial features (endotoxin pathways); plant foods and fish were associated with SCFA-producing anti-inflammatory bacteria. This gives the food-level rationale for MD.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Plant foods and fish, the backbone of MD, are associated with anti-inflammatory microbiome features.

Title: TNF compromises intestinal bile-acid tolerance dictating colitis progression and limited infliximab response
Focus: Cell Metabolism 2024 (mouse and human). A high-fat diet worsens colitis because TNF disables bile-acid detoxification in gut epithelium. High intestinal bile acids correlated with poor INFLIXIMAB response, and clearing bile acids improved infliximab efficacy in mice.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Hypothesis-generating diet-drug link. A lower-saturated-fat diet such as MD lowers primary bile acids (see Godny 2025), which could in theory support anti-TNF response. This has not yet been tested in patients.

Title: The potential role of the mediterranean diet on clinical outcomes in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: A systematic review
Focus: 2026 systematic review (12 studies, 1,615 patients). Observational studies link MD adherence to lower inflammatory markers, better quality of life and less disease activity, but RCT effects on biomarkers were mixed and mostly non-significant. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.
Link to Mediterranean diet: The most up-to-date, balanced summary: promising for quality of life and remission, but RCT evidence is still limited.

Title: Effects of the Mediterranean diet on inflammation, quality of life, and mortality in autoimmune diseases: A systematic review featured in the Italian National Guidelines "La Dieta Mediterranea"
Focus: Systematic review for the Italian national MD guidelines (autoimmune diseases including CD and UC). MD is associated with better quality of life and possibly lower CRP, and one cohort showed lower mortality in IBD. Certainty is low.

Title: Is the Mediterranean Diet in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases Ready for Prime Time?
Focus: Narrative review: 'Is the MD in IBD ready for prime time?' It concludes that the current evidence may support integrating MD into IBD care, citing lower risk, clinical improvement, lower markers, better quality of life and lower mortality, while asking for phenotype-specific trials.

Title: Diet and clinical remission in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: A multicenter cross-sectional study
Focus: Cross-sectional study across 40 French and Belgian centres (2025). Higher MD adherence was associated with CD remission (aOR 1.39) but not UC remission. Fruit, coffee and salad intake were also associated with remission. Reverse causality is possible.

Title: Dietary management in inflammatory bowel disease: A narrative review of the current evidence
Focus: 2026 narrative review anchored on the ECCO 2025 dietary consensus. No single IBD diet fits all. EEN or CDED+PEN for active CD; fibre linked to lower relapse; MD supports UC remission maintenance; do not routinely restrict fibre or dairy; limit UPF and red meat; monitor micronutrients.
Link to Mediterranean diet: Practical, phase-specific summary showing where MD fits within the whole dietary toolbox.
